question: can you explain gradient descent in 3d surface

slides.title: The Loss Surface

parameters.description: 3D surface z=x^2+2y^2 over x,y in [-3,3], with x and y base axes, vertical z axis labelled loss, and minimum marked at (0,0,0).

slides.caption: z=f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2
slides.narration: Think of the loss as height above the x-y plane. The surface z equals x squared plus 2y squared is a bowl, and its lowest point is at the origin.

slides.title: Choose a Starting Point

parameters.description: Retain the 3D bowl z=x^2+2y^2 over x,y in [-3,3]. Mark the surface point (3,2,22), label it current point (3,2), and project it vertically to (3,2,0).

slides.caption: (x_0,y_0)=(3,2)
slides.narration: To make the descent concrete, start at the surface point whose horizontal coordinates are x zero equals 3 and y zero equals 2.

slides.title: Measure the Slope
slides.caption: \nabla f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}2x\\4y\end{bmatrix}
slides.narration: The gradient collects the rate of change in the x direction and the rate of change in the y direction. Differentiating gives 2x and 4y.

slides.title: The Gradient Points Uphill
slides.caption: -\nabla f(x,y)=\begin{bmatrix}-2x\\-4y\end{bmatrix}
slides.narration: The gradient points in the direction where the loss rises fastest. To reduce the loss, we travel in the opposite direction.

slides.title: The Update Rule
slides.caption: (x_{k+1},y_{k+1})=(x_k,y_k)-\eta\nabla f(x_k,y_k)
slides.narration: At each step, multiply the gradient by the learning rate eta, then subtract that vector from the current coordinates. This produces the next point.

slides.title: First Downhill Step
slides.caption: (x_1,y_1)=(3-0.1(2\cdot3),\;2-0.1(4\cdot2))=(2.4,1.2)
slides.narration: At the starting coordinates, the gradient is 6 in x and 8 in y. With eta equal to 0.1, subtracting the scaled gradient moves the point to 2.4 comma 1.2.

slides.title: The x-Coordinate Shrinks
slides.caption: x:\;3,\;2.4,\;1.92,\;1.536,\;1.2288,\;0.98304
slides.narration: Repeating the x update gives 3, 2.4, 1.92, 1.536, 1.2288, and 0.98304. The x coordinate steadily moves toward zero.

slides.title: The y-Coordinate Shrinks Faster
slides.caption: y:\;2,\;1.2,\;0.72,\;0.432,\;0.2592,\;0.15552
slides.narration: The y sequence is 2, 1.2, 0.72, 0.432, 0.2592, and 0.15552. It contracts faster because the surface is steeper in the y direction.

slides.title: Every Step Lowers the Loss
slides.caption: f(x-0.1(2x),y-0.1(4y))=0.64x^2+0.72y^2
slides.narration: After one update, the loss becomes 0.64x squared plus 0.72y squared. Both coefficients are smaller than before, so every nonzero point loses height for this learning rate.

slides.title: Convergence to the Minimum
slides.caption: \lim_{k\to\infty}(x_k,y_k)=(0,0)
slides.narration: As the point gets closer to the bottom, the gradient gets smaller. The steps shrink, and the coordinates converge to zero.

slides.title: The Complete Descent

parameters.description: Show the complete 3D surface z=x^2+2y^2 over x,y in [-3,3], axes, start point (3,2,22), connected trajectory points with the verified sequences, negative-gradient arrows, and minimum (0,0,0) labelled z=0.

slides.caption: \text{plot }z=x^2+2y^2\text{ together with }(x_k,y_k,f(x_k,y_k))
slides.narration: The whole process is now visible: the path begins at (3,2), follows negative-gradient directions down the bowl, and approaches the minimum at the origin, where the loss is zero.

slides.title: FINAL ANSWER
slides.caption: \boxed{(x_{k+1},y_{k+1})=(x_k,y_k)-\eta\begin{bmatrix}2x_k\\4y_k\end{bmatrix},\qquad \eta=0.1}
slides.narration: The gradient-descent rule is the current point minus eta times the gradient. Here eta is 0.1, generating a descending sequence from (3,2) toward the minimum (0,0,0).
